title: Submission intake automation pricing: why you should pay on submissions, not policies
summary: How the billing unit decides whether submission intake automation pays back. A pricing guide for commercial P&C carriers and MGAs.
body_markdown:
When you buy submission intake automation, the pricing choice that matters most is whether the solution is priced on the submissions you receive or on the policies you bind, and in almost every case pricing on submissions received is the better option because it makes the cost predictable before you know your hit ratio. Most buyers compare feature lists and monthly license fees first, although the pricing model underneath has a bigger effect, since it decides who carries the risk when volume spikes or a document type gets messy.


According to the CIAB Commercial Market Index, commercial property rates are softening in 2026, with non-catastrophe accounts down 4% to 10%. Submission volumes keep climbing while underwriting headcount stays flat, which means carriers now process more intake for less premium, and every dollar of intake cost lands on the expense side of the[combined ratio](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/combined-ratio) . A pricing model that scales with the wrong number slowly widens that ratio. This guide explains how[submission intake automation](https://pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-automation-insurance) is priced, why the billing unit matters and which cost drivers are worth checking before you sign.


## How is submission intake automation priced?


Submission intake automation is usually priced in one of four ways, and each one bills against a different unit of work. The unit you choose decides how your cost behaves as volume, document complexity and bind rate change over the year.


Pricing model How cost scales Best fit What to watch


Per submission received Tracks your actual intake volume and stays predictable per account. Carriers and MGAs with high submission-to-bind ratios. You pay on declines too, which matches the cost to the work done.


Per document or per page Multiplies by the document count per submission, which you don't control. Low-document, single-LOB books. A 200-tab SOV or a thick loss run can spike the cost of one submission.


Per seat or license Fixed by user count and flat against volume. Small teams with steady, modest intake. Cost per submission drops only if each seat processes more, which often doesn't happen.


Managed-service subscription Annual fee per program, sized to volume and complexity. Teams that want the review labor included in the fee. Confirm the accuracy guarantee and review scope are written into the contract.


Pibit AI prices on the submissions we process, so you pay for every submission that reaches the inbox, whatever your bind rate turns out to be, with no license fee and no implementation fee, and the ROI we commit to is written into the contract. Each of the six stages of the AI Underwriting OS can be bought on its own, which lets you buy the[intake and clearance](https://pibit.ai/intake-and-clearance) function you need now and add the rest later.


## Why price on submissions received instead of policies bound?


Pricing on submissions received ties the cost to the work and keeps the budget predictable, since intake work happens on every submission and only some of them get bound. A model tied to bound policies or premium hides the real cost of clearing declines and out-of-appetite accounts, which still take up intake time.


Here is a simple example. Say you receive 20,000 submissions a year and bind 4,000 of them: a submissions-received model bills on 20,000, which is the volume your team actually touches and a number you can forecast before the year starts. A premium-linked or policy-linked model ties your tooling cost to an outcome that shifts with market rates and hit ratio, two things you can't fully control, and when[volume rises while rates soften](https://pibit.ai/blog/es-submission-volume-soft-rates-throughput-problem) , that kind of pricing can drift away from the work being done.


Per-policy pricing bills 4,000 units for 20,000 submissions of intake work; the 16,000 submissions that are not bound take the same work and are not counted


Per-document pricing has the opposite problem, because it scales with a number the broker sets. A clean BOP submission and a 200-tab[statement of values](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/statement-of-values-sov) cost the same to quote from your side, yet per-document pricing charges very different amounts for them, which makes the expense line hard to plan.


## What drives the cost up or down?


Five factors move the price more than the headline rate does, and volume is only one of them. Document complexity, line of business, the number of modules and the exception rate each change the real cost per submission.


Cost driver Why it moves the price Question to ask


Submission volume The base unit. Higher volume lowers the per-submission rate at most tiers. Does the rate step down as annual volume grows?


Document complexity Large SOVs, multi-year[loss runs](https://pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/loss-run) and handwritten forms take more work. Is complex extraction included, or billed as an overage?


Lines of business Each LOB needs its own appetite rules and field mapping. Is each new LOB a change order or part of the base?


Modules deployed Intake, extraction, research and scoring can be bought separately. Can you start with one module and expand without repricing?


Exception rate Low-confidence fields route to human review, and that review is labor. Who pays for the review: you, or the vendor under the accuracy SLA?


## Is the review work included in the price?


This is worth checking before anything else, because it is where pricing models split in two. An AI-only tool gives you extraction and leaves the checking to your team, while a managed model includes the review and owns the accuracy number, so two quotes with similar sticker prices can lead to very different total costs.


In Pibit AI's experience,[AI extraction](https://pibit.ai/extraction-and-research) on its own lands at around 90% to 95% field-level accuracy on varied commercial documents, and that is the best case for most vendors. At that level[95% is not production ready](https://pibit.ai/blog/underwriting-accuracy-commercial-pc-95-percent-production-ready) , so someone still has to review every field, and if that person is your underwriting assistant, the license fee was only part of the cost, with the rest paid in staff hours and slower quotes.


Pibit AI includes the review in the price through an AI services model, where our AI agents check every field and human experts step in when needed, so your underwriters receive clean data and never work a review queue. That model guarantees 99.9% field-level accuracy with our human-in-the-loop, written into the contract, which means you aren't paying for a license and then paying again to fix the output. Multi-step review that keeps edge cases honest is the reason[a contractual 99.9% guarantee beats an unverified accuracy claim](https://pibit.ai/blog/ai-underwriting-accuracy-benchmark-99-percent) .


## How do you calculate the payback?


Compare the annual fee against three numbers you already track: rework cost, freed capacity and loss-ratio drift. The payback rarely comes from cutting the tooling line, and it usually comes from what accurate, faster intake does to the P&L.


Rework is the place to start, since a single misread on a large account moves real money: a $50,000 error on a $2M fleet account shifts the loss ratio on that account by about 2.5 points, and catching a handful of those a year pays for the tool. The[real cost of inaccurate underwriting data](https://pibit.ai/blog/real-cost-inaccurate-underwriting-data-commercial-p-c) shows up in loss-ratio points far more than in data-entry hours.


Capacity is the second number. Clean intake gives underwriters time for risk selection instead of keystrokes, and Pibit AI has delivered a[20% increase in hit ratio](https://pibit.ai/casestudies/how-camico-drove-a-20-increase-in-new-business-hit-ratio) , 70% faster time to quote and a 2x increase in underwriter throughput. Those results are what a payback case rests on, more than the per-submission rate.


## What hidden costs should you check before you sign?


Four line items rarely show up in the headline price, and each one can change the real cost per submission after go-live. Asking about them up front helps you avoid paying twice for the same work.


- Integration. Pibit AI integrates with existing policy admin systems, including Guidewire, Duck Creek and Insurity, with no rip-and-replace, and typical integration takes a few weeks from scope lock. Ask whether integration is included and how long it takes, since a long build costs money even when it isn't on the invoice.
- Overages on complex documents, such as large SOVs and multi-year loss runs.
- Change orders for each new line of business.
- Accuracy rework when the guarantee is soft. A 95% best-effort target pushes the review cost onto your team, while a 99.9% guarantee written into the contract keeps it with the vendor.


When you weigh[build versus buy](https://pibit.ai/blog/build-vs-buy-underwriting-automation) , an internal build carries the same hidden costs, minus the vendor's accountability for them.


Price works best as the last question you ask. Settle the billing unit, confirm the review is included and pressure-test the accuracy guarantee, and the number on the quote becomes easy to defend.
